reply:
The question is ambiguous: "average transaction amount per customer" most naturally means, for each customer, the average of their transaction amounts. The relevant table is Sales.CustomerTransactions, which has CustomerID and TransactionAmount, so I'll group by customer and average. I'll join to Sales.Customers to include the customer name.

```sql
SELECT c.CustomerID,
       c.CustomerName,
       AVG(ct.TransactionAmount) AS avg_transaction_amount
FROM Sales.CustomerTransactions ct
JOIN Sales.Customers c ON c.CustomerID = ct.CustomerID
GROUP BY c.CustomerID, c.CustomerName
ORDER BY c.CustomerID;
```

Customers link to a state/province through their delivery city: Sales.Customers.DeliveryCityID → Application.Cities.CityID → Application.StateProvinces.StateProvinceID. I'll use the delivery city, which matches the Website.Customers view, and count customers per state province name.

```sql
SELECT sp.StateProvinceName,
       COUNT(c.CustomerID) AS customer_count
FROM Sales.Customers c
JOIN Application.Cities ci ON c.DeliveryCityID = ci.CityID
JOIN Application.StateProvinces sp ON ci.StateProvinceID = sp.StateProvinceID
GROUP BY sp.StateProvinceName
ORDER BY customer_count DESC, sp.StateProvinceName;
```

The question doesn't name a table, so I assumed it means customer transactions. "Completed successfully" is taken to mean a finalized transaction (`IsFinalized = true`), and the amount is `TransactionAmount`. If you meant supplier transactions, the same query works against `Purchasing.SupplierTransactions`.

```sql
SELECT AVG(TransactionAmount) AS avg_completed_transaction_amount
FROM Sales.CustomerTransactions
WHERE IsFinalized = true;
```

The "account name" here refers to the customer name, and the account opening date is `AccountOpenedDate` in `Sales.Customers`. To get the single earliest opened account, I sort by that date ascending and take one row. A tie-breaker on `CustomerID` keeps the result deterministic when several accounts share the same date.

```sql
SELECT CustomerName
FROM Sales.Customers
ORDER BY AccountOpenedDate ASC, CustomerID ASC
LIMIT 1;
```

Quantity sold per stock item is best taken from invoice lines, since those record what was actually sold. Grouping by stock item and averaging the quantity gives the result. I join to StockItems to show the item name, using an inner join so every returned item has a name. Items with no sales won't appear.

```sql
SELECT si.StockItemID,
       si.StockItemName,
       AVG(il.Quantity) AS average_quantity_sold
FROM Sales.InvoiceLines AS il
JOIN Warehouse.StockItems AS si ON si.StockItemID = il.StockItemID
GROUP BY si.StockItemID, si.StockItemName
ORDER BY si.StockItemID;
```

Customers who had backorders: in Sales.Orders, an order that has a backorder is linked via BackorderOrderID (the order that was created as the backorder). Orders with BackorderOrderID IS NOT NULL are the originals that spawned a backorder. Counting distinct customers on those rows gives the number of customers who had backorders.

```sql
SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT CustomerID) AS customers_with_backorders
FROM Sales.Orders
WHERE BackorderOrderID IS NOT NULL;
```

Black Friday 2024 is Friday, 2024-11-29. The schema has no promotion flag on orders, so I treat an order as "with promotion" when at least one of its lines matches a `SpecialDeals` row that is active on the order date. A deal matches if its stock item, customer, buying group, customer category and stock group are either null (not restricted) or equal to the line's values. Order value is the sum of `Quantity * UnitPrice` over the order's lines.

```sql
WITH bf_orders AS (
    SELECT o.OrderID,
           EXISTS (
               SELECT 1
               FROM Sales.OrderLines ol2
               JOIN Sales.Customers c ON c.CustomerID = o.CustomerID
               JOIN Sales.SpecialDeals sd
                 ON o.OrderDate BETWEEN sd.StartDate AND sd.EndDate
                AND (sd.StockItemID IS NULL OR sd.StockItemID = ol2.StockItemID)
                AND (sd.CustomerID IS NULL OR sd.CustomerID = o.CustomerID)
                AND (sd.BuyingGroupID IS NULL OR sd.BuyingGroupID = c.BuyingGroupID)
                AND (sd.CustomerCategoryID IS NULL OR sd.CustomerCategoryID = c.CustomerCategoryID)
                AND (sd.StockGroupID IS NULL OR EXISTS (
                        SELECT 1
                        FROM Warehouse.StockItemStockGroups sisg
                        WHERE sisg.StockItemID = ol2.StockItemID
                          AND sisg.StockGroupID = sd.StockGroupID))
               WHERE ol2.OrderID = o.OrderID
           ) AS has_promotion
    FROM Sales.Orders o
    WHERE o.OrderDate = DATE '2024-11-29'
),
order_values AS (
    SELECT b.OrderID,
           b.has_promotion,
           SUM(ol.Quantity * ol.UnitPrice) AS order_value
    FROM bf_orders b
    JOIN Sales.OrderLines ol ON ol.OrderID = b.OrderID
    GROUP BY b.OrderID, b.has_promotion
)
SELECT CASE WHEN has_promotion THEN 'With promotion' ELSE 'Without promotion' END AS promotion_status,
       COUNT(*) AS order_count,
       ROUND(AVG(order_value), 2) AS average_order_value
FROM order_values
GROUP BY has_promotion
ORDER BY has_promotion DESC;
```

Revenue is best taken from invoice lines, since they hold the sold amounts. Each invoice line's ExtendedPrice is the line total including tax, and the invoice date comes from Sales.Invoices. Credit notes would be negative, but in this dataset invoice lines are the standard measure of sales.

Two options for "revenue":
- Sum of ExtendedPrice (includes tax).
- Sum of ExtendedPrice minus TaxAmount (excludes tax), which is true revenue.

I'll use the excluding-tax figure, since tax collected isn't revenue: ExtendedPrice - TaxAmount, which equals Quantity * UnitPrice.

Q1 2013 covers 2013-01-01 through 2013-03-31 inclusive, so I'll filter on `InvoiceDate >= '2013-01-01' AND InvoiceDate < '2013-04-01'`.

```sql
SELECT SUM(il.ExtendedPrice - il.TaxAmount) AS total_revenue
FROM Sales.InvoiceLines il
JOIN Sales.Invoices i ON i.InvoiceID = il.InvoiceID
WHERE i.InvoiceDate >= DATE '2013-01-01'
  AND i.InvoiceDate < DATE '2013-04-01';
```

Approach: an order counts as a backorder when `BackorderOrderID` is not null. I took the year from `OrderDate` and counted distinct customers per year. I used `generate_series` for 2000–2020 so that years with no backorders still appear with a count of 0.

```sql
SELECT y.year,
       COUNT(DISTINCT o.CustomerID) AS customers_with_backorders
FROM generate_series(2000, 2020) AS y(year)
LEFT JOIN Sales.Orders o
       ON EXTRACT(YEAR FROM o.OrderDate)::int = y.year
      AND o.BackorderOrderID IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY y.year
ORDER BY y.year;
```

The question is ambiguous, so I read "stock count" as the number of stock items per brand. I count rows in `Warehouse.StockItems` grouped by `Brand`, exclude items with no brand, and take the top 10. If you meant total units on hand, the query would instead sum `QuantityOnHand` from `Warehouse.StockItemHoldings`.

```sql
SELECT Brand,
       COUNT(*) AS stock_count
FROM Warehouse.StockItems
WHERE Brand IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY Brand
ORDER BY stock_count DESC, Brand
LIMIT 10;
```

Approach: find invoice lines for stock items whose Brand is 'Northwind', join through invoices to customers, sum the quantity per customer, and take the top one.

"Biggest consumer" is best read as the customer who bought the largest total quantity. Credit notes are not specially handled, since the question doesn't mention them.

```sql
SELECT c.CustomerID, c.CustomerName, SUM(il.Quantity) AS total_quantity
FROM Sales.InvoiceLines il
JOIN Warehouse.StockItems si ON si.StockItemID = il.StockItemID
JOIN Sales.Invoices i ON i.InvoiceID = il.InvoiceID
JOIN Sales.Customers c ON c.CustomerID = i.CustomerID
WHERE si.Brand = 'Northwind'
GROUP BY c.CustomerID, c.CustomerName
ORDER BY total_quantity DESC
LIMIT 1;
```

Orders are stored in `Sales.Orders`, and `OrderDate` is a `date` column. Filtering on equality with 2013-11-01 returns every order placed that day.

```sql
SELECT *
FROM Sales.Orders
WHERE OrderDate = DATE '2013-11-01'
ORDER BY OrderID;
```

Order value = sum of OrderLines Quantity * UnitPrice per order. Average per order, grouped by customer category.

Steps:
1. Compute each order's value from Sales.OrderLines (Quantity * UnitPrice).
2. Join orders to customers, then to customer categories.
3. Average the order totals per category.

```sql
WITH order_values AS (
    SELECT o.OrderID,
           o.CustomerID,
           SUM(ol.Quantity * ol.UnitPrice) AS order_value
    FROM Sales.Orders o
    JOIN Sales.OrderLines ol ON ol.OrderID = o.OrderID
    GROUP BY o.OrderID, o.CustomerID
)
SELECT cc.CustomerCategoryName,
       AVG(ov.order_value) AS average_order_value
FROM order_values ov
JOIN Sales.Customers c ON c.CustomerID = ov.CustomerID
JOIN Sales.CustomerCategories cc ON cc.CustomerCategoryID = c.CustomerCategoryID
GROUP BY cc.CustomerCategoryName
ORDER BY average_order_value DESC;
```

The question doesn't define "delay", so I took it as the gap between the promised and actual delivery dates. That is `Invoices.ConfirmedDeliveryTime` minus `Orders.ExpectedDeliveryDate`. Each invoice links to its order, and the customer's delivery city comes from `Customers.DeliveryCityID`. I averaged the delay in days per city, ignoring invoices with no confirmed delivery time, and kept the 5 cities with the largest average.

```sql
SELECT c.CityName,
       AVG(EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM (i.ConfirmedDeliveryTime - o.ExpectedDeliveryDate::timestamp)) / 86400.0) AS avg_delay_days
FROM Sales.Invoices i
JOIN Sales.Orders o ON o.OrderID = i.OrderID
JOIN Sales.Customers cu ON cu.CustomerID = i.CustomerID
JOIN Application.Cities c ON c.CityID = cu.DeliveryCityID
WHERE i.ConfirmedDeliveryTime IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY c.CityID, c.CityName
ORDER BY avg_delay_days DESC
LIMIT 5;
```

The question asks for the ratio of salespeople to employees in Application.People. Salespeople are flagged by IsSalesperson and employees by IsEmployee.

The ratio is the count of salespeople divided by the count of employees. I use `COUNT(*) FILTER` for each count and cast to numeric to avoid integer division. `NULLIF` guards against division by zero.

One ambiguity is whether "employees" means everyone with IsEmployee = true (which includes salespeople) or only non-salesperson employees. In this schema, salespeople are also employees, so the straightforward reading is salespeople over all employees.

```sql
SELECT
    COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE IsSalesperson)::numeric
    / NULLIF(COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE IsEmployee), 0) AS salesperson_to_employee_ratio
FROM Application.People;
```

The schema has no explicit discount column on invoices or invoice lines, so I treated "bought with discount" as an invoice line sold at a unit price below the stock item's list price. The query counts distinct customers with at least one such line on an invoice dated in 2024. Credit notes are excluded. The WideWorldImporters sample data mostly predates 2024, so this may return 0.

```sql
SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT i.CustomerID) AS customers_with_discount_2024
FROM Sales.Invoices i
JOIN Sales.InvoiceLines il ON il.InvoiceID = i.InvoiceID
JOIN Warehouse.StockItems si ON si.StockItemID = il.StockItemID
WHERE i.InvoiceDate >= DATE '2024-01-01'
  AND i.InvoiceDate < DATE '2025-01-01'
  AND i.IsCreditNote = false
  AND il.UnitPrice < si.UnitPrice;
```

Suppliers don't sell directly in this schema. Their stock items are sold to customers through invoice lines. So I join suppliers to their stock items, then to the invoice lines for those items, and sum the quantity sold per supplier. I take the top 5 by that total.

```sql
SELECT s.SupplierID,
       s.SupplierName,
       SUM(il.Quantity) AS total_items_sold
FROM Purchasing.Suppliers s
JOIN Warehouse.StockItems si ON si.SupplierID = s.SupplierID
JOIN Sales.InvoiceLines il ON il.StockItemID = si.StockItemID
GROUP BY s.SupplierID, s.SupplierName
ORDER BY total_items_sold DESC
LIMIT 5;
```

The only vehicle-related data is in `Warehouse.VehicleTemperatures`, where each vehicle is identified by `VehicleRegistration`. Since that table has many readings per vehicle, I count the distinct registrations.

```sql
SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT VehicleRegistration) AS number_of_vehicles
FROM Warehouse.VehicleTemperatures;
```

The question asks for the average unit price of stock items grouped by size. The relevant table is `Warehouse.StockItems`, which has both `Size` and `UnitPrice`. Grouping by `Size` gives one row per size, and items with a NULL size are grouped together as one NULL group.

```sql
SELECT Size,
       AVG(UnitPrice) AS average_unit_price
FROM Warehouse.StockItems
GROUP BY Size
ORDER BY Size;
```

`Warehouse.StockItems` holds the stock items, and its `TaxRate` column is where a tax rate is attached. I read "doesn't have a tax rate attached" as `TaxRate IS NULL`. The column is declared `NOT NULL`, so this will return 0 unless the schema is changed.

```sql
SELECT COUNT(*) AS items_without_tax_rate
FROM Warehouse.StockItems
WHERE TaxRate IS NULL;
```

There's no search log table in this schema, so I treated the tags on each stock item as its search terms. `Warehouse.StockItems.Tags` holds a JSON array of tags. The query expands those arrays, counts how many stock items carry each tag, and returns the 6 most common.

```sql
SELECT t.search_term,
       COUNT(*) AS item_count
FROM Warehouse.StockItems si
CROSS JOIN LATERAL jsonb_array_elements_text(
    CASE WHEN si.Tags IS NULL OR btrim(si.Tags) = '' THEN '[]'::jsonb ELSE si.Tags::jsonb END
) AS t(search_term)
GROUP BY t.search_term
ORDER BY item_count DESC, t.search_term
LIMIT 6;
```

Suppliers have a DeliveryCityID that links to Application.Cities. I'll group by city and count suppliers, then take the top 5. Grouping by CityID avoids merging distinct cities that share a name, and I'll order ties by city name to keep results deterministic.

```sql
SELECT c.CityName, COUNT(*) AS supplier_count
FROM Purchasing.Suppliers s
JOIN Application.Cities c ON s.DeliveryCityID = c.CityID
GROUP BY c.CityID, c.CityName
ORDER BY supplier_count DESC, c.CityName
LIMIT 5;
```

Interpretation: for each city that has suppliers, compute population divided by the number of suppliers in it (using the delivery city), and return the 5 highest ratios.

Steps:
1. Join Application.Cities to Purchasing.Suppliers on DeliveryCityID.
2. Group by city and count the suppliers.
3. Divide LatestRecordedPopulation by the supplier count.
4. Sort descending and take the top 5.

```sql
SELECT c.CityID,
       c.CityName,
       c.LatestRecordedPopulation,
       COUNT(s.SupplierID) AS supplier_count,
       c.LatestRecordedPopulation::numeric / COUNT(s.SupplierID) AS population_per_supplier
FROM Application.Cities c
JOIN Purchasing.Suppliers s ON s.DeliveryCityID = c.CityID
WHERE c.LatestRecordedPopulation IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY c.CityID, c.CityName, c.LatestRecordedPopulation
ORDER BY population_per_supplier DESC
LIMIT 5;
```

Approach: "Items ordered by customers" means the quantity on order lines, so I sum Sales.OrderLines.Quantity per Sales.Orders.OrderDate. Then I take the day with the highest total.

Summing Quantity counts units ordered. Counting lines would count distinct products instead, so I use the sum. Ties are broken by returning all tied days via `RANK`.

```sql
SELECT OrderDate, total_items
FROM (
    SELECT o.OrderDate,
           SUM(ol.Quantity) AS total_items,
           RANK() OVER (ORDER BY SUM(ol.Quantity) DESC) AS rnk
    FROM Sales.Orders o
    JOIN Sales.OrderLines ol ON ol.OrderID = o.OrderID
    GROUP BY o.OrderDate
) t
WHERE rnk = 1;
```

The data has no direct link between a deal and the sales it produced. I therefore defined "most successful" as the deal with the highest order revenue (quantity × unit price). A deal counts an order line only if all of these hold:

- The order date falls within the deal's start and end dates.
- The line matches every criterion the deal sets: stock item, stock group, customer, buying group and customer category. A criterion left empty (NULL) on the deal matches anything.

```sql
SELECT sd.SpecialDealID,
       sd.DealDescription,
       SUM(ol.Quantity * ol.UnitPrice) AS total_revenue,
       COUNT(DISTINCT o.OrderID) AS order_count,
       SUM(ol.Quantity) AS total_quantity
FROM Sales.SpecialDeals sd
JOIN Sales.Orders o
  ON o.OrderDate BETWEEN sd.StartDate AND sd.EndDate
JOIN Sales.Customers c
  ON c.CustomerID = o.CustomerID
JOIN Sales.OrderLines ol
  ON ol.OrderID = o.OrderID
WHERE (sd.StockItemID IS NULL OR sd.StockItemID = ol.StockItemID)
  AND (sd.CustomerID IS NULL OR sd.CustomerID = o.CustomerID)
  AND (sd.BuyingGroupID IS NULL OR sd.BuyingGroupID = c.BuyingGroupID)
  AND (sd.CustomerCategoryID IS NULL OR sd.CustomerCategoryID = c.CustomerCategoryID)
  AND (sd.StockGroupID IS NULL OR EXISTS (
        SELECT 1
        FROM Warehouse.StockItemStockGroups sisg
        WHERE sisg.StockItemID = ol.StockItemID
          AND sisg.StockGroupID = sd.StockGroupID))
GROUP BY sd.SpecialDealID, sd.DealDescription
ORDER BY total_revenue DESC
LIMIT 1;
```

I read "best sellers" as the stock items with the highest total quantity sold on invoices. I took "North America" to mean `Application.Countries.Continent`, since the `Region` column holds "Americas" instead. Each invoice is placed in a country through the customer's delivery city, then its state/province, then its country. I haven't run the query against the database.

```sql
SELECT si.StockItemID,
       si.StockItemName,
       SUM(il.Quantity) AS total_quantity_sold
FROM Sales.InvoiceLines il
JOIN Sales.Invoices i ON i.InvoiceID = il.InvoiceID
JOIN Sales.Customers c ON c.CustomerID = i.CustomerID
JOIN Application.Cities ci ON ci.CityID = c.DeliveryCityID
JOIN Application.StateProvinces sp ON sp.StateProvinceID = ci.StateProvinceID
JOIN Application.Countries co ON co.CountryID = sp.CountryID
JOIN Warehouse.StockItems si ON si.StockItemID = il.StockItemID
WHERE co.Continent = 'North America'
GROUP BY si.StockItemID, si.StockItemName
ORDER BY total_quantity_sold DESC, si.StockItemID
LIMIT 4;
```

The question is ambiguous, so I read "geographical area" as the sales territory and "targets" as where the most customers are located. Each customer's delivery city links to a state/province, which carries the `SalesTerritory`. I count customers per territory and keep the top 3.

```sql
SELECT sp.SalesTerritory,
       COUNT(c.CustomerID) AS customer_count
FROM Sales.Customers c
JOIN Application.Cities ci ON ci.CityID = c.DeliveryCityID
JOIN Application.StateProvinces sp ON sp.StateProvinceID = ci.StateProvinceID
GROUP BY sp.SalesTerritory
ORDER BY customer_count DESC, sp.SalesTerritory
LIMIT 3;
```

Count orders per customer in Sales.Orders, keep those with more than 130, and join to Sales.Customers for the name.

```sql
SELECT c.CustomerID, c.CustomerName, COUNT(o.OrderID) AS order_count
FROM Sales.Customers c
JOIN Sales.Orders o ON o.CustomerID = c.CustomerID
GROUP BY c.CustomerID, c.CustomerName
HAVING COUNT(o.OrderID) > 130
ORDER BY order_count DESC;
```

Orders link to customers, and customers link to buying groups. So I join Orders to Customers, then to BuyingGroups, and count orders per group.

I use an inner join to BuyingGroups, which leaves out customers with no buying group. A LEFT JOIN from BuyingGroups would also list groups that have no orders, and COUNT of the order ID would give them 0.

```sql
SELECT bg.BuyingGroupID,
       bg.BuyingGroupName,
       COUNT(o.OrderID) AS order_count
FROM Sales.BuyingGroups bg
LEFT JOIN Sales.Customers c ON c.BuyingGroupID = bg.BuyingGroupID
LEFT JOIN Sales.Orders o ON o.CustomerID = c.CustomerID
GROUP BY bg.BuyingGroupID, bg.BuyingGroupName
ORDER BY bg.BuyingGroupName;
```

The cold room temperature readings are in `Warehouse.ColdRoomTemperatures`. The columns `RecordedWhen` (timestamp) and `Temperature` give what was asked. I'll include the sensor number for context and order the results chronologically.

```sql
SELECT RecordedWhen, Temperature
FROM Warehouse.ColdRoomTemperatures
ORDER BY RecordedWhen;
```

Interpretation: "sale transactions" are rows in Sales.CustomerTransactions. The question asks for the month with the most of them. I'm grouping by calendar month (year and month together) and counting rows.

An alternative would be to group by month of the year across all years. "The month" most naturally means a specific month such as 2015-03, so I'm using year-month.

```sql
SELECT DATE_TRUNC('month', TransactionDate)::date AS sale_month,
       COUNT(*) AS transaction_count
FROM Sales.CustomerTransactions
GROUP BY DATE_TRUNC('month', TransactionDate)
ORDER BY transaction_count DESC
LIMIT 1;
```

This reads "purchase totals" as the value of purchase orders placed in 2014, grouped by supplier. Each order line is valued as ordered outers × expected unit price per outer. If you meant invoiced amounts from `SupplierTransactions` instead, the query would need to change.

```sql
SELECT s.SupplierID,
       s.SupplierName,
       SUM(pol.OrderedOuters * pol.ExpectedUnitPricePerOuter) AS total_purchases_2014
FROM Purchasing.PurchaseOrders po
JOIN Purchasing.PurchaseOrderLines pol ON pol.PurchaseOrderID = po.PurchaseOrderID
JOIN Purchasing.Suppliers s ON s.SupplierID = po.SupplierID
WHERE po.OrderDate >= DATE '2014-01-01'
  AND po.OrderDate < DATE '2015-01-01'
GROUP BY s.SupplierID, s.SupplierName
ORDER BY total_purchases_2014 DESC;
```

Invoices are in Sales.Invoices, and InvoiceDate is a date column. I filter on a half-open range covering May 2014 (from 2014-05-01 up to but not including 2014-06-01), which returns every invoice dated in that month.

```sql
SELECT InvoiceID, CustomerID, InvoiceDate
FROM Sales.Invoices
WHERE InvoiceDate >= DATE '2014-05-01'
  AND InvoiceDate < DATE '2014-06-01'
ORDER BY InvoiceDate, InvoiceID;
```

The question asks for a monthly summary of total sales, built from the chiller and dry item counts on invoices. "Grouped by invoice date" is ambiguous. Since the summary is monthly, I'll truncate InvoiceDate to the month and group by that.

The totals come from Sales.Invoices: TotalChillerItems and TotalDryItems. I'll return each of them per month, plus their combined total.

```sql
SELECT
    DATE_TRUNC('month', InvoiceDate)::date AS invoice_month,
    SUM(TotalChillerItems) AS total_chiller_items,
    SUM(TotalDryItems) AS total_dry_items,
    SUM(TotalChillerItems + TotalDryItems) AS total_items_sold
FROM Sales.Invoices
GROUP BY DATE_TRUNC('month', InvoiceDate)
ORDER BY invoice_month;
```

The question asks for the total discount amount per deal description, which comes from the `Sales.SpecialDeals` table. I group by `DealDescription` and sum `DiscountAmount`. Rows with a NULL `DiscountAmount` (percentage-based deals) are ignored by SUM, so a description whose deals all have NULL amounts returns NULL. I'm keeping that behavior rather than coercing it to 0.

```sql
SELECT DealDescription,
       SUM(DiscountAmount) AS total_discount_amount
FROM Sales.SpecialDeals
GROUP BY DealDescription;
```

Sales.CustomerTransactions has a TransactionAmount column, which already includes tax (AmountExcludingTax + TaxAmount). So the average transaction amount including tax per customer is the average of TransactionAmount grouped by CustomerID. I'll join to Sales.Customers to include the customer name.

```sql
SELECT c.CustomerID,
       c.CustomerName,
       AVG(ct.TransactionAmount) AS avg_transaction_amount_including_tax
FROM Sales.CustomerTransactions ct
JOIN Sales.Customers c ON c.CustomerID = ct.CustomerID
GROUP BY c.CustomerID, c.CustomerName
ORDER BY c.CustomerID;
```

The question asks for "order details" with customer names, so I joined the order lines (the detail rows) to their orders and then to customers. The link is `OrderLines.OrderID` → `Orders.OrderID`, and `Orders.CustomerID` → `Customers.CustomerID`.

```sql
SELECT o.OrderID,
       o.OrderDate,
       c.CustomerName,
       ol.OrderLineID,
       ol.StockItemID,
       ol.Description,
       ol.Quantity,
       ol.UnitPrice,
       ol.TaxRate,
       ol.PickedQuantity
FROM Sales.Orders AS o
JOIN Sales.Customers AS c ON c.CustomerID = o.CustomerID
JOIN Sales.OrderLines AS ol ON ol.OrderID = o.OrderID
ORDER BY o.OrderID, ol.OrderLineID;
```

Sum TransactionAmount per customer from Sales.CustomerTransactions, join to Sales.Customers for the name, order by the total descending, and keep the top 100.

```sql
SELECT c.CustomerID,
       c.CustomerName,
       SUM(ct.TransactionAmount) AS TotalTransactionAmount
FROM Sales.CustomerTransactions ct
JOIN Sales.Customers c ON c.CustomerID = ct.CustomerID
GROUP BY c.CustomerID, c.CustomerName
ORDER BY TotalTransactionAmount DESC
LIMIT 100;
```

Order details are the rows in Sales.OrderLines, and each row has a StockItemID. Joining that to Warehouse.StockItems gives the stock item name. I also join Sales.Orders so each line shows its order date and customer.

```sql
SELECT ol.OrderLineID,
       ol.OrderID,
       o.CustomerID,
       o.OrderDate,
       ol.StockItemID,
       si.StockItemName,
       ol.Description,
       ol.PackageTypeID,
       ol.Quantity,
       ol.UnitPrice,
       ol.TaxRate,
       ol.PickedQuantity,
       ol.PickingCompletedWhen
FROM Sales.OrderLines ol
JOIN Sales.Orders o ON o.OrderID = ol.OrderID
JOIN Warehouse.StockItems si ON si.StockItemID = ol.StockItemID
ORDER BY ol.OrderID, ol.OrderLineID;
```

Join Purchasing.SupplierTransactions to Purchasing.Suppliers on SupplierID to get each transaction together with its supplier's name.

```sql
SELECT st.*, s.SupplierName
FROM Purchasing.SupplierTransactions AS st
JOIN Purchasing.Suppliers AS s ON s.SupplierID = st.SupplierID
ORDER BY st.SupplierTransactionID;
```

This query treats an order line as having a special deal when a deal's date range covers the order date. The deal must also match the customer side (customer, buying group or customer category) and the item side (stock item or stock group). A deal column left NULL is treated as "applies to all". I have not run it against the database.

```sql
SELECT o.OrderID,
       o.OrderDate,
       o.CustomerID,
       ol.OrderLineID,
       ol.StockItemID,
       ol.Description,
       ol.Quantity,
       ol.UnitPrice,
       ol.TaxRate,
       sd.SpecialDealID,
       sd.DealDescription,
       sd.StartDate,
       sd.EndDate,
       sd.DiscountAmount,
       sd.DiscountPercentage,
       sd.UnitPrice AS DealUnitPrice
FROM Sales.Orders AS o
JOIN Sales.OrderLines AS ol ON ol.OrderID = o.OrderID
JOIN Sales.Customers AS c ON c.CustomerID = o.CustomerID
JOIN Sales.SpecialDeals AS sd
  ON o.OrderDate BETWEEN sd.StartDate AND sd.EndDate
 AND (
        (sd.CustomerID IS NULL AND sd.BuyingGroupID IS NULL AND sd.CustomerCategoryID IS NULL)
     OR sd.CustomerID = o.CustomerID
     OR sd.BuyingGroupID = c.BuyingGroupID
     OR sd.CustomerCategoryID = c.CustomerCategoryID
     )
 AND (
        (sd.StockItemID IS NULL AND sd.StockGroupID IS NULL)
     OR sd.StockItemID = ol.StockItemID
     OR EXISTS (
          SELECT 1
          FROM Warehouse.StockItemStockGroups AS sisg
          WHERE sisg.StockItemID = ol.StockItemID
            AND sisg.StockGroupID = sd.StockGroupID
        )
     )
```
